name: Use RuntimeClasses in workloads
objective: CKS › Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities. Drill EVERY RuntimeClass corner harder than the exam: create a class and its required handler, the optional scheduling/overhead fields, select it per-pod and per-Deployment, contrast with the default runtime, layer securityContext hardening on top, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Harden the sandboxed pod (defence in depth)
questions.teach:
A sandbox is one layer — stack **securityContext** hardening for defence in depth: **drop ALL capabilities** (container `securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`) and **run non-root** (`runAsNonRoot: true` + `runAsUser: 1000`), while keeping `spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor`.

**Gotcha:** `capabilities` is **container-level** — putting it in the pod `securityContext` is a silent no-op.
questions.prompt:
Replace pod `sandboxed` in `runtimeclass-learn` so it still requests `runtimeClassName: gvisor` AND its container drops **ALL** capabilities and runs non-root (`runAsNonRoot: true`, `runAsUser: 1000`). Keep image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`.

Target: `sandboxed` has runtimeClassName `gvisor`, `runAsNonRoot: true`, `runAsUser: 1000`, and its container's `capabilities.drop` contains `ALL`.
questions.hint: Delete and re-apply YAML with `spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor`, pod `securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000 }`, and the container's `securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`. busybox sleep runs fine as uid 1000.
questions.solution:
kubectl delete pod sandboxed -n runtimeclass-learn --ignore-not-found
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: sandboxed, namespace: runtimeclass-learn }
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
YAML

verification.description: 'sandboxed' keeps gvisor AND runs non-root (uid 1000) AND drops ALL caps

questions.eli5:
A sandbox is great, but good security isn't one wall — it's **several walls**, so if an attacker gets past one, the next still stops them. Security people call this "defence in depth." You already gave the pod a sandbox (gVisor). Now you add two more cheap, strong walls on top using **securityContext**.

Think of it like locking a car *and* putting the valuables in the boot *and* parking in a guarded garage:

- **Drop ALL capabilities** — Linux "capabilities" are little superpowers a process can have (change the clock, open raw sockets, etc.). Most apps need none. Dropping `ALL` strips every superpower, so even a hijacked process can do almost nothing.
- **Run as non-root** — `runAsNonRoot: true` plus `runAsUser: 1000` makes the container run as an ordinary user, not the all-powerful root. If something breaks out, it's a nobody, not an admin.

The trap is **where** each setting goes. Dropping capabilities is a **container-level** setting (`capabilities` lives in the *container's* `securityContext`). If you put `capabilities` in the *pod's* `securityContext` instead, Kubernetes just ignores it silently — you *think* you're protected but you're not. Meanwhile `runAsNonRoot`/`runAsUser` can live at the pod level (and apply to all containers) or the container level.

**Watch out for:**

- **`capabilities` is container-level only** — putting `drop: ["ALL"]` in the *pod* `securityContext` is a **silent no-op**; nest it under the container's `securityContext`.
- Keep `spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor` — the hardening is *in addition to* the sandbox, not a replacement.
- `runAsNonRoot: true` *rejects* the pod at start if the image would run as root — pair it with `runAsUser: 1000` so a concrete non-root uid is set.
- `drop: ["ALL"]` is the string `ALL` in a list — exact spelling, uppercase.
- busybox `sleep` runs fine as uid 1000; some images break as non-root — know your image.
- You must **delete and re-apply** the pod (most fields are immutable) to change it.
questions.deepDive:
## Hardening a sandboxed pod (defence in depth) — full rundown

### Mental model
A sandbox runtime (gVisor/Kata) is **one** isolation layer. CKS wants **layered** controls so a single bypass isn't game over: keep the sandbox **and** apply `securityContext` hardening — drop Linux capabilities, run as a non-root uid, and (ideally) a read-only rootfs and no privilege escalation. Each control is independent; together they shrink the blast radius.

### Pod vs container securityContext — the critical split
`securityContext` exists at **two levels**, and some fields are valid at only one:

| Field | Pod `spec.securityContext` | Container `securityContext` | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `runAsNonRoot` | ✅ | ✅ | container overrides pod |
| `runAsUser` / `runAsGroup` | ✅ | ✅ | container overrides pod |
| `fsGroup` | ✅ | ❌ | pod-only (volume ownership) |
| `capabilities` | ❌ | ✅ | **container-only** — pod-level is ignored |
| `readOnlyRootFilesystem` | ❌ | ✅ | container-only |
| `allowPrivilegeEscalation` | ❌ | ✅ | container-only |
| `seccompProfile` | ✅ | ✅ | both |

**`capabilities` in the pod securityContext is a silent no-op** — the #1 trap here.

### The target manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: sandboxed, namespace: runtimeclass-learn }
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor          # keep the sandbox
  securityContext:                  # pod-level: applies to all containers
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:                # container-level
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]               # strip every Linux capability
      # readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      # allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
```

### Linux capabilities, briefly
Capabilities split root's power into units (`CAP_NET_RAW`, `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, …). Default containers start with a handful. **`drop: ["ALL"]`** removes them all; add back only what's needed with `add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]`. Most workloads need none — least privilege.

### runAsNonRoot vs runAsUser
- `runAsNonRoot: true` — kubelet **refuses to start** a container whose effective user is root (uid 0); a guard, not an assignment.
- `runAsUser: 1000` — actually **sets** the uid. Pair them: `runAsNonRoot` enforces, `runAsUser` provides the concrete non-root id so the guard is satisfied deterministically.

### Changing an existing pod
Most pod fields (including `securityContext`, `runtimeClassName`) are **immutable**:
```bash
kubectl delete pod sandboxed -n runtimeclass-learn --ignore-not-found
kubectl apply -f sandboxed.yaml      # recreate with hardening
```

### Verifying
```bash
kubectl -n runtimeclass-learn get pod sandboxed -o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}{"\n"}'          # gvisor
kubectl -n runtimeclass-learn get pod sandboxed -o jsonpath='{.spec.securityContext.runAsUser}{"\n"}' # 1000
kubectl -n runtimeclass-learn get pod sandboxed -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext.capabilities.drop}{"\n"}' # ["ALL"]
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`capabilities` is container-level** — pod-level placement is ignored silently. Verify under `.spec.containers[].securityContext`.
- **Keep `runtimeClassName: gvisor`** — hardening complements the sandbox; dropping it loses a layer.
- `runAsNonRoot: true` without a non-root uid can crash a root image at start with `CreateContainerConfigError`; set `runAsUser: 1000`.
- `drop: ["ALL"]` — list with the exact uppercase string `ALL`; don't write `all` or a bare `ALL`.
- Pods are **immutable** for these fields — delete and recreate; `kubectl edit` is rejected.
- Container-level securityContext **overrides** pod-level for overlapping fields.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
  securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000 }
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
```

questions.title: Select a RuntimeClass from a Deployment
questions.teach:
For controllers, `runtimeClassName` lives in the **pod template** — `spec.template.spec.runtimeClassName` — so every replica gets the sandbox. It is NOT a field on the Deployment's own `spec`.

**Gotcha:** setting it at `deployment.spec.runtimeClassName` (outside the template) is rejected/ignored — it must be inside `template.spec`.
questions.prompt:
In `runtimeclass-learn`, create a Deployment `sandboxed-web` with 2 replicas, container `c` running `nginx:1.25`, whose pod template requests `runtimeClassName: gvisor`.

Target: Deployment `sandboxed-web` has 2 replicas and `.spec.template.spec.runtimeClassName` = `gvisor`.
questions.hint: Put `runtimeClassName: gvisor` under `spec.template.spec` (sibling of `containers`), not on the Deployment spec. Set `spec.replicas: 2`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: sandboxed-web, namespace: runtimeclass-learn }
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: sandboxed-web } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: sandboxed-web } }
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: gvisor
      containers:
      - name: c
        image: nginx:1.25
YAML
questions.eli5:
You rarely run one lonely pod in production — you run a **Deployment** that keeps, say, 2 identical copies alive. So how do you make *every* copy use the sandbox? You set the runtime class on the **blueprint** the Deployment stamps out, not on the Deployment itself.

Picture a Deployment as a cookie cutter. The `template` is the cookie-cutter *shape* — every cookie (pod) comes out matching it. If you want all cookies to be "sandboxed," you put `runtimeClassName: gvisor` into the **template's** pod spec (`spec.template.spec.runtimeClassName`). Then all 2 replicas inherit it.

The classic mistake is putting `runtimeClassName` on the Deployment's own top-level `spec` (`deployment.spec.runtimeClassName`). That's like writing on the cookie cutter's *handle* instead of its *shape* — it doesn't belong there. Kubernetes ignores/rejects it, and your pods come out with the default runtime. The field is a **pod** field, so it only makes sense **inside the pod template**.

**Watch out for:**

- `runtimeClassName` goes in **`spec.template.spec`** (the pod template), a sibling of `containers` — **not** on the Deployment's own `spec`.
- Putting it at `deployment.spec.runtimeClassName` is **ignored/rejected** — wrong level.
- Set `spec.replicas: 2` and make sure the `selector.matchLabels` match the template's pod labels, or the Deployment won't come up.
- Every replica inherits the template, so all pods get the sandbox automatically — and new ones from scaling/rollout too.
- Same caveat as before: without `runsc` installed the replicas may stay Pending; the graded signal is the template field + replica count.
questions.deepDive:
## Selecting a RuntimeClass from a Deployment — full rundown

### Mental model
`runtimeClassName` is a **pod** field. Controllers (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job) don't run pods directly — they own a **pod template** (`spec.template`) and stamp pods from it. So to make every replica sandboxed, you set `runtimeClassName` **inside the template's pod spec** (`spec.template.spec.runtimeClassName`), exactly where you'd set it on a bare pod. The Deployment's own `spec` has no such field.

### Where it goes
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: sandboxed-web, namespace: runtimeclass-learn }
spec:
  replicas: 2                         # Deployment-level
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: sandboxed-web }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: sandboxed-web }  # MUST match selector
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: gvisor        # <-- pod field, inside template.spec
      containers:
      - name: c
        image: nginx:1.25
```

### Field-level map
| Setting | Correct path |
|---|---|
| replica count | `spec.replicas` |
| label selector | `spec.selector.matchLabels` |
| pod labels | `spec.template.metadata.labels` |
| **runtimeClassName** | `spec.template.spec.runtimeClassName` |
| containers | `spec.template.spec.containers` |

Putting `runtimeClassName` at `spec.runtimeClassName` (Deployment level) is **not a valid field** — the API server rejects it (strict) or it's dropped, and pods come up on the default runtime.

### selector ↔ template labels
The `selector.matchLabels` must be a subset of `template.metadata.labels`, or the API server rejects the Deployment ("selector does not match template labels"). This is unrelated to RuntimeClass but a frequent co-occurring failure.

### Verifying
```bash
kubectl -n runtimeclass-learn get deploy sandboxed-web \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}{" "}{.spec.template.spec.runtimeClassName}{"\n"}'   # 2 gvisor

kubectl -n runtimeclass-learn get pods -l app=sandboxed-web \
  -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,RC:.spec.runtimeClassName
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`runtimeClassName` lives in `spec.template.spec`**, not on the Deployment `spec`. Wrong level = ignored/rejected, pods default-runtime.
- It's a **pod field** — same semantics as a bare pod, just templated; all replicas inherit it, including ones created by scaling/rollouts.
- Ensure `selector.matchLabels` ⊆ `template.metadata.labels` or the Deployment is rejected.
- With `runsc` absent, replicas may be **Pending/ContainerCreating** — graded signal is `replicas: 2` + `template.spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor`, not Running.
- Same template rule applies to StatefulSet/DaemonSet/Job — always inside `template.spec`.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: sandboxed-web } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: sandboxed-web } }
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: gvisor     # pod template
      containers:
      - { name: c, image: nginx:1.25 }
```
```bash
kubectl -n runtimeclass-learn get deploy sandboxed-web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}{" "}{.spec.template.spec.runtimeClassName}'; echo
```

questions.title: List and confirm both classes coexist
questions.teach:
A cluster can expose **several** RuntimeClasses so workloads pick the isolation they need; `kubectl get runtimeclass` lists them all. The class **name** (what pods reference) and the **`handler`** (what the CRI maps to a binary) are separate fields.

**Gotcha:** deleting a RuntimeClass does NOT touch pods already referencing it — they keep their `runtimeClassName` string, which simply won't resolve on the next schedule.
questions.prompt:
Confirm the cluster exposes BOTH classes you built: `gvisor` (handler `runsc`) and `kata` (handler `kata`), coexisting.

Target: `kubectl get runtimeclass` lists both `gvisor` and `kata` with their correct handlers (`runsc` and `kata`).
questions.hint: This passes once steps 1 and 2 are done. Verify with `kubectl get runtimeclass` and `kubectl get runtimeclass gvisor kata -o jsonpath='{.items[*].handler}'`.
questions.eli5:
A cluster isn't limited to one runtime option. You can offer a whole **menu** of RuntimeClasses, and each workload picks the isolation it needs: maybe `gvisor` for one team's risky jobs, `kata` (a lightweight VM) for another's. This step is just confirming both of the classes you built earlier are sitting there side by side, ready to be chosen.

`kubectl get runtimeclass` prints the menu. You should see both `gvisor` and `kata`, each with its own **handler** — the behind-the-scenes binary name. Two things to keep straight: the class **name** is what pods type into `runtimeClassName`; the **handler** is what the container runtime actually launches. They're separate columns and often differ (`gvisor` → `runsc`, while `kata` → `kata`).

One sharp edge to remember: RuntimeClasses and the pods using them are **loosely coupled**. If you *delete* a RuntimeClass, Kubernetes does **not** go clean up or stop the pods already using it — those pods keep their `runtimeClassName` string. It just won't resolve the *next* time one tries to schedule, and then it breaks. So deleting a class is quietly dangerous.

**Watch out for:**

- The **name** (what pods reference) and the **handler** (CRI binary) are different fields — `gvisor`→`runsc`, `kata`→`kata`.
- Deleting a RuntimeClass does **NOT** touch pods already referencing it — they keep the string, which simply fails to resolve on the next schedule.
- RuntimeClasses are **cluster-scoped** — list with `kubectl get runtimeclass`, no namespace.
- Multiple classes coexist happily; a cluster can offer several isolation levels at once.
- This step passes only once the earlier steps (creating `gvisor` and `kata`) are done — it's a confirmation, not new work.
questions.deepDive:
## Multiple RuntimeClasses coexisting — full rundown

### Mental model
A cluster can expose **as many RuntimeClasses as the nodes support**, giving workloads a menu of isolation levels. Each class is an independent, cluster-scoped object mapping a **name** (the pod-facing handle) to a **handler** (the CRI-facing runtime key). Classes don't conflict; a pod picks exactly one by name. Operators publish classes like `gvisor` and `kata`; teams choose per-workload.

### name vs handler — two distinct fields
| Field | Who uses it | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `metadata.name` | pods/templates via `runtimeClassName` | `gvisor`, `kata` |
| `handler` | the node's CRI → runtime binary | `runsc`, `kata` |

They are decoupled and often differ (`gvisor` → `runsc`). Two classes may even share a handler if two names should map to the same runtime.

### Listing and confirming
```bash
kubectl get runtimeclass                     # cluster-scoped list of all classes
kubectl get runtimeclass gvisor kata         # just the two

# handlers for both, in order
kubectl get runtimeclass gvisor kata \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"="}{.handler}{"\n"}{end}'
# gvisor=runsc
# kata=kata
```

### Lifecycle coupling (the trap)
RuntimeClass and the pods referencing it are **loosely coupled**:
- Deleting a RuntimeClass **does not** delete, stop, or mutate pods already running with it — they keep their `runtimeClassName` string unchanged.
- The deletion only bites on the **next scheduling** of a pod that names the now-missing class: admission rejects it ("RuntimeClass … not found"), so it never schedules.
- Running pods continue until they're rescheduled/recreated (node drain, rollout, crash) — then they fail to come back.

This is why removing a class in use is quietly destabilising: no immediate error, delayed failure.

### Why multiple classes
- `gvisor` (`runsc`): user-space kernel, strong syscall interposition, low overhead vs VMs.
- `kata` (`kata`): micro-VM per pod, hardware-virtualization boundary, higher overhead.
- default `runc`: shared kernel, lowest overhead.

Different trust levels → different classes, selected per workload.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **name ≠ handler** — pods reference the name; the CRI resolves the handler. Confirm both columns.
- RuntimeClass is **cluster-scoped** — `kubectl get runtimeclass`, never `-n`.
- **Deleting a class doesn't clean up its pods** — they keep the string and break only on reschedule. Don't assume deletion is safe while workloads reference it.
- A pod/template referencing a **non-existent** class is rejected at admission; a class whose **handler is missing on the node** fails at the kubelet.
- This confirmation step depends on the earlier `gvisor`/`kata` creation steps already passing.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl get runtimeclass
kubectl get runtimeclass gvisor kata \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}={.handler}{"\n"}{end}'
# gvisor=runsc
# kata=kata
```
